# Payment gateway integration hub: architecture and system design

← [Capstone brief](../README.md) · [All capstones](../../README.md)

One internal API in front of several payment providers: initialisation with failover, signed webhooks, a strict payment state machine, idempotency, refunds and reconciliation.

Five views of the same system, from the business context down to the cloud. Read them in order: each answers a different question that system-design interviews ask. Every diagram is provided as **Mermaid** (renders on GitHub), **draw.io / diagrams.net** XML (open and edit at [app.diagrams.net](https://app.diagrams.net)), **SVG** and **PNG**.

## 1. Solution architecture

![Payment gateway integration hub: solution architecture](solution.svg)

**Solution architecture**: merchant applications integrate once with the hub; the hub integrates with each payment provider. Providers call back with signed webhooks. Keycloak issues the merchants' tokens; operations watch provider health and payments.

## 2. Logical architecture

![Payment gateway integration hub: logical architecture](logical.svg)

**Logical architecture**: three flows share one payment record. *Initialise* checks the idempotency key, picks a provider through the router and stores the payment as `PENDING`. *Webhooks* are verified (HMAC over the raw body), de-duplicated by provider event id and applied through the state machine. *Reconciliation* verifies stale pending payments. Every transition appends an immutable payment event.

        hook["Webhook intake<br/>signature · dedup"]
        sm["Payment state machine<br/>legal transitions only"]
        recon[["Reconciliation<br/>verify stale · abandon"]]
        refund["Refunds<br/>never above amount"]
    end
    subgraph sg1["Data (PostgreSQL)"]
        direction TB
        payment[("payment<br/>reference · merchant · amount · status")]

        idem[("idempotency_key<br/>merchant · key · request hash · response")]

    end

## 3. Technical architecture

![Payment gateway integration hub: technical architecture (inside the service)](technical.svg)

**Technical architecture** shows *how the code is organised* inside the Spring Boot 4 service: thin controllers that validate and translate errors, services that hold the business rules and transaction boundaries, and a persistence layer (JPA where entity behaviour and locking help, `JdbcClient`/SQL for reporting and bulk work). Cross-cutting concerns (configuration, health, metrics, scheduling, outbound HTTP) are framework features configured once. Package by feature in code; the layers here are logical.

## 4. Infrastructure architecture

![Payment gateway integration hub: infrastructure architecture (VPS)](infra.svg)

**Infrastructure architecture** shows *where things run* on the cheapest production-like target, a single VPS (for example SSDNodes). Only Caddy is reachable from the internet; it terminates TLS and forwards to `payment-gateway-hub` on Docker's internal network, so the database is never exposed (Docker port publishing bypasses `ufw`, so nothing else publishes ports). Images are built once by GitHub Actions, stored in GHCR by commit SHA, and pulled onto the server; backups leave the machine daily. Keycloak is published on its own subdomain through Caddy so users and client apps can obtain tokens; the API only fetches its public signing keys (JWKS) and validates tokens locally. Sizing and every command are in the [deployment guide](../../../deploy/README.md#3-deploy-to-a-vps).

## 5. Cloud architecture

![Payment gateway integration hub: cloud architecture (AWS reference, Azure/GCP equivalents)](cloud.svg)

**Cloud architecture** maps the service onto managed cloud building blocks, drawn for AWS (ECS Express Mode, the AWS-recommended path for new accounts since App Runner closed to new customers in 2026). The database sits in private subnets; credentials come from the secret store, never from the image; images are immutable and tagged by commit SHA. The same design on the other clouds:

| AWS | Azure | GCP |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL | Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server | Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL |
| ECS Express Mode (Fargate) | Azure Container Apps | Cloud Run |
| Amazon ECR | Azure Container Registry | Artifact Registry |
| AWS Secrets Manager | Azure Key Vault | Secret Manager |
| CloudWatch | Azure Monitor / Log Analytics | Cloud Logging & Monitoring |
| EventBridge Scheduler | Container Apps jobs | Cloud Scheduler |
| Keycloak on ECS / Amazon Cognito | Keycloak on Container Apps / Microsoft Entra ID | Keycloak on Cloud Run / Identity Platform |

Step-by-step setup for all three: [deployment guide](../../../deploy/README.md).

## Use these in your own capstone

Copy this folder into your repository, then change the diagrams to match what you actually built. In interviews, walk through the solution view first, then the logical view, then answer deep-dive questions with the technical, infrastructure and cloud views. Write a new ADR whenever you make a decision a future teammate would ask "why?" about.
